summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Danish criminal law and Danish passport and document rules apply here; equality and family law are set by the Faroese Løgting under a Danish human-rights framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1933, when it was legalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

The only criminal provision in force that touches LGBT people is the anti-discrimination law that took effect on 1 January 2007. It makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Its enactment made the Faroe Islands the last country in Northern Europe to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation. The provision as recorded covers sexual orientation; gender identity is not named as a protected ground in the source material.

Before that law, no Faroese statute addressed discrimination against sexual minorities, and that gap shaped how complaints were handled. In 2006 an openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host, Rasmus Rasmussen, was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012.

Violence against visibly LGBT visitors and performers has been documented. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group reported it had been attacked nowhere else.

Religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures is openly present in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion. In 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned, compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

In June 2015 the Speaker of the Løgting, Jógvan á Lakjuni, published a letter to the editor attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as "non-culture", asking whether "these people do not feel any shame".

The first gay pride march, in 2005, provoked much controversy.
tangentialFactors:
The Faroe Islands lagged its Nordic neighbours on this area of law: it was the last country in Northern Europe to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation, and it retained an age of consent of 18 for male same-sex relations until 1988, eleven years after Denmark moved to a gender-neutral age of 15.

The only criminal penalty recorded in the source material for LGBT-related conduct attaches to public statements that threaten, insult or degrade a group, with a maximum of two years' imprisonment. No provision recorded here criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression.

Cultural venues have been a flashpoint: a drag show at the Nordic House drew a public attack from the Speaker of the Løgting in 2015, and the first pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy.
localsOnly:
Organised petitioning has been a recurring feature of Faroese LGBT politics. In 2006 activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; the territory had neither at that date. After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen an internet petition collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

When Jenis av Rana demanded in 2015 that Pride be banned, two days before the national holiday, the singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not record the current status of marriage or registered-partnership recognition in the Faroe Islands, nor whether gender identity is a protected ground under the 2007 anti-discrimination law.

No source in the inventory addresses Faroese rules on identity documents and gender markers, entry and visa processing, airport or border screening, access to transition-related healthcare, or the use of gendered facilities. Enforcement data for the 2007 anti-discrimination provision is likewise not sourced.

The documented incidents of anti-LGBT violence are individual cases; the inventory provides no rate and no comparison with the territory's general violent-crime rate.
